layers.title: Dutch register: immigration by origin country
layers.question: How many people of this origin registered as immigrants in the Netherlands this month?
layers.note: Immigration is a registration event, not an arrival: a person is counted once a municipality enters them in the population register, which requires an expected stay of at least four months. Herkomstland is the migrant's own country of birth, or their parents' if they were born in the Netherlands, so this is a count of people by origin and not a flow from a place: 14.1% of the 23,148 registrations in 2026-07 were of people born in the Netherlands, and nothing in this table records where any of them travelled from.

layers.title: Dutch register: emigration by origin country
layers.question: How many people of this origin left the Dutch register this month?
layers.note: This is emigration net of the balance of administrative corrections — CBS's preferred series, because most departures are never declared and surface later as administrative removals — so a cell is a net register movement and not a count of departures, and 114 of the 13,031 cells here are negative. Herkomstland is the migrant's own country of birth, or their parents' if they were born in the Netherlands, so this is a count of people by origin and not a flow from a place: 21.0% of the 24,524 net register departures in 2026-07 were of people born in the Netherlands, and nothing in this table records where any of them travelled from.

layers.title: Beneficiaries of temporary protection
layers.question: How many people held temporary protection here at the end of the month?
layers.note: A stock at the end of each month, not a flow: summing it across months counts the same person once per month they stayed.

layers.title: Temporary protection beneficiaries by citizenship
layers.question: How many citizens of this country held temporary protection in that one?
layers.note: Almost entirely one corridor set: Ukrainians are 1,250,825 of Germany’s 1,286,840 beneficiaries at 2026-06, so this answers a different question from asylum and must not be added to it.

layers.title: Temporary protection granted
layers.question: How many people were newly granted temporary protection here this month?
layers.note: A monthly flow of first grants; France is flagged throughout as measuring this to a different definition.

layers.title: Canada: permanent residents admitted
layers.question: How many people of this citizenship were granted permanent residence in Canada?
layers.note: An admission is the grant of permanent-resident status, not a move. Many of the people counted here were already living in Canada on a study or work permit and did not travel on the day they were admitted, so this is not the same measurement as a European population register and the two should not be differenced. The axis is country of citizenship, an attribute of the person rather than of the journey, which is why there is no corridor layer. IRCC rounds every count to the nearest 5 and withholds counts of 1-5 as '--': in 2026-07 28 of the 217 citizenship rows are withheld and are absent here rather than zero, while 46 rows carry a literal 0 that is a real zero — the workbook's own note claiming 0-5 are all shown as '--' is contradicted by its own data. 141 citizenships have a non-zero figure in 2026-07; a row count would say 217 and overstate it. Quarter and year totals in the sheet are discarded, including the trailing 'Q3 Total' column that currently holds July alone. Rows with no country to key on are excluded: Stateless 250, Other 5 in 2026-07.

layers.title: Canada: asylum claims received
layers.question: How many people of this citizenship lodged an asylum claim in Canada?
layers.note: Claims received in the month, by the claimant’s country of citizenship — an event, not a stock of people waiting, and not a decision. Citizenship is an attribute of the person and says nothing about where they travelled from, so there is no corridor layer. Only 25 citizenships are in this file at all: IRCC publishes the top 25 of the NEWEST month — 2026-07 — and then carries that one ranking back across the whole 139-month history, so everyone outside it sits in an unnamed residual for every month, and a citizenship that was large years ago but small now never appears. Rebuilding this layer in a later month will change which countries have history. The residual held 1,015 claims in 2026-07 against 2,920 across the named countries. The published cells are province-by-month counts rounded to 5 with counts of 1-5 withheld as '--', and IRCC titles the file itself "[rounded numbers - not for calculations]" for that reason; each national figure here is a sum of those cells, so it is a lower bound — 52 withheld province cells sit under the named countries in 2026-07, hiding between 52 and 260 claims. A citizenship-month whose every province cell was withheld is left out rather than recorded as zero. Claims lodged outside Canada are counted here under the citizenship, the same as any other.

layers.title: EU asylum applications
layers.question: How many people asked this country for asylum?
layers.note: Applications lodged, first-time and repeat together; Spain is flagged provisional throughout 2026 and its fall from 8,275 in 2026-05 to 3,005 in 2026-06 should not be read as an outturn.

layers.title: EU first-time asylum applications
layers.question: How many people asked this country for asylum for the first time?
layers.note: FRST excludes repeat applications; FRST + SSEQ is the TOTAL layer, so never add this to it.

layers.title: EU asylum applications by citizenship
layers.question: How many citizens of this country applied for asylum in that one?
layers.note: Origin is citizenship, not country of departure, and a corridor absent here was never reported rather than reported as none.

layers.title: EU first-instance asylum decisions
layers.question: How many first-instance decisions did this country issue?
layers.note: Decisions issued, not applications resolved into them; Greece carries a break in series at 2025-Q4 and Spain is provisional from 2025-Q1 onwards.

layers.title: EU positive first-instance decisions
layers.question: How many first-instance decisions granted some form of protection?
layers.note: POS already contains refugee status, humanitarian status and subsidiary protection; adding the three POS_* codes to it double-counts every grant.

layers.title: EU first-instance decisions by citizenship
layers.question: How many first-instance decisions did that country issue to citizens of this one?
layers.note: All decision types together, so a large corridor says nothing about how many of those decisions granted protection; at geo=DE, 2026-Q2 only 101 of the 206 citizenships carry a non-zero value.

layers.title: Temporary protection granted, quarterly
layers.question: How many people were newly granted temporary protection here this quarter?
layers.note: The quarterly cut of the monthly grants table, published on a slower cycle and including Montenegro, which the monthly table omits.

layers.title: Protection status withdrawn
layers.question: How many first-instance protection statuses did this country withdraw?
layers.note: Withdrawals at first instance for any reason including a status simply ending; Germany quintupled from 1,015 in 2025-Q4 to 5,020 in 2026-Q2, which is a policy change and not a data error.

layers.title: Asylum applications pending
layers.question: How many applications were still awaiting a first-instance decision here?
layers.note: A stock of open cases at the end of the month, not a flow; Italy and Portugal had not filed for 2026-06, so the layer sums 21% below 2026-05 for that reason alone, Italy is flagged low-reliability from 2025-03 to 2026-04, and Spain is provisional throughout.

layers.title: Personal transfers received
layers.question: How much money did households here receive from abroad this quarter?
layers.note: Personal transfers — "current transfers between resident and nonresident households" in the IMF's own words — received by resident households from non-resident households, in current US dollars, a proxy for what this country's emigrants send home. It is money, not people, and it is NOT BILATERAL: this dataflow has no counterpart-country dimension, so nothing here says where the money came from or went, and pairing one country's figure with another's invents the corridor. 2026-Q1 is an incomplete quarter by construction — 87 countries have reported against a trailing median of 114, because BOP coverage keeps accumulating for years after a reference period. A country missing here has not reported yet; it has not reported zero. 1 country publishes an exact zero at 2026-Q1 (DEU). That is a published value rather than an absence, and against a non-zero previous quarter it is the commonest way a first release reads as a collapse — check the quarter before it and the same country's next revision before quoting it. DNK is dropped rather than drawn: it has never published a non-zero figure in any quarter it files inside this layer's window. Such a series can stop decades before the window does (DNK's ends in 1993), so that is "never non-zero wherever it reports", not "filed a zero for every quarter this layer covers". A zero filed quarter after quarter is a reporting convention, not a measurement. Current dollars are not deflated and not exchange-rate adjusted, so a rise can be prices or a currency move. It is narrower than "remittances": the IMF's own personal remittances item (R1_S1W) adds compensation of employees, and at 2026-Q1 it ran between 1.17 and 3.16 times this one across the four countries that published both. That ratio is a one-off measurement taken on 2026-09-20, not a figure this layer recomputes, so read it as the order of magnitude of what personal transfers leaves out rather than as a current number. Only four countries publish R1_S1W at all, which is why it cannot be shipped instead.

layers.title: Personal transfers sent
layers.question: How much money did households here send abroad this quarter?
layers.note: Personal transfers — "current transfers between resident and nonresident households" in the IMF's own words — sent by resident households to non-resident households, in current US dollars, a proxy for what immigrants living here send out. It is money, not people, and it is NOT BILATERAL: this dataflow has no counterpart-country dimension, so nothing here says where the money came from or went, and pairing one country's figure with another's invents the corridor. 2026-Q1 is an incomplete quarter by construction — 89 countries have reported against a trailing median of 118, because BOP coverage keeps accumulating for years after a reference period. A country missing here has not reported yet; it has not reported zero. DNK, HND, LSO, TUR are dropped rather than drawn: they have never published a non-zero figure in any quarter they file inside this layer's window. Such a series can stop decades before the window does (DNK's ends in 1993), so that is "never non-zero wherever it reports", not "filed a zero for every quarter this layer covers". A zero filed quarter after quarter is a reporting convention, not a measurement. Current dollars are not deflated and not exchange-rate adjusted, so a rise can be prices or a currency move. It is narrower than "remittances": the IMF's own personal remittances item (R1_S1W) adds compensation of employees, and at 2026-Q1 it ran between 1.17 and 3.16 times this one across the four countries that published both. That ratio is a one-off measurement taken on 2026-09-20, not a figure this layer recomputes, so read it as the order of magnitude of what personal transfers leaves out rather than as a current number. Only four countries publish R1_S1W at all, which is why it cannot be shipped instead.

layers.title: German register: moves in and out, by partner country
layers.question: How many people moved along this corridor in 2025, as Germany recorded it?
layers.note: Germany's municipal population register, table 12711-05 of the Statistischer Bericht Wanderungen 2025, counted by country of previous or next residence rather than by citizenship, so a cell is a move between two places. Individual counts are perturbed for disclosure control by the cell-key method — the workbook says so in footnote * and it shows: male plus female misses the published total in 175 of 418 partner-direction cells, by up to 4 people — so never rebuild a total by summing parts and never rescale the parts to a total. Two entries are wider than the code they are filed under: China includes Hong Kong and Macau, and Sudan includes the pre-2011 Sudan alongside a separate South Sudan row. The same two corridors appear on the Italian layers from Italy's own register: at 2025 Italy to Germany is 38,812 (Germany) against 14,583 (Italy), 2.66x and Germany to Italy is 36,848 (Germany) against 12,835 (Italy), 2.87x. Neither register is wrong; they count different events. A German Abmeldung is transacted at a counter people must visit to end their tax and tenancy obligations, while Italian emigration is recorded through AIRE consular enrolment that emigrants frequently never complete. Read the pair as a measurement of how incomplete emigration statistics are, not as two estimates to average.

layers.title: Italian register: moves in and out, by partner country
layers.question: How many people moved along this corridor in 2025, as Italy recorded it?
layers.note: Italy's municipal population register (anagrafe), counted by country of previous or next residence. Every 2025 cell carries OBS_STATUS "p": these are provisional and ISTAT revises them. Emigration in particular is understood to be undercounted, because leaving the register requires the emigrant to enrol with AIRE at a consulate and many never do. The same two corridors appear on the German layers from Germany's own register: at 2025 Italy to Germany is 38,812 (Germany) against 14,583 (Italy), 2.66x and Germany to Italy is 36,848 (Germany) against 12,835 (Italy), 2.87x. Read the pair as a measurement of how incomplete emigration statistics are, not as two estimates to average.

layers.title: German register: arrivals from abroad, by country left
layers.question: How many people moved to Germany from this country in 2025?
layers.note: Germany's municipal population register, table 12711-05 of the Statistischer Bericht Wanderungen 2025, counted by country of previous or next residence rather than by citizenship, so a cell is a move between two places. Individual counts are perturbed for disclosure control by the cell-key method — the workbook says so in footnote * and it shows: male plus female misses the published total in 175 of 418 partner-direction cells, by up to 4 people — so never rebuild a total by summing parts and never rescale the parts to a total. Two entries are wider than the code they are filed under: China includes Hong Kong and Macau, and Sudan includes the pre-2011 Sudan alongside a separate South Sudan row. Germany recorded no partner country at all for 134,408 arrivals (9.1% of 1,479,944) and 210,182 departures (16.9% of 1,244,944) in 2025; those moves are absent from this layer rather than distributed across it, so the country values do not sum to German migration.

layers.title: German register: departures abroad, by country moved to
layers.question: How many people left Germany for this country in 2025?
layers.note: Germany's municipal population register, table 12711-05 of the Statistischer Bericht Wanderungen 2025, counted by country of previous or next residence rather than by citizenship, so a cell is a move between two places. Individual counts are perturbed for disclosure control by the cell-key method — the workbook says so in footnote * and it shows: male plus female misses the published total in 175 of 418 partner-direction cells, by up to 4 people — so never rebuild a total by summing parts and never rescale the parts to a total. Two entries are wider than the code they are filed under: China includes Hong Kong and Macau, and Sudan includes the pre-2011 Sudan alongside a separate South Sudan row. Germany recorded no partner country at all for 134,408 arrivals (9.1% of 1,479,944) and 210,182 departures (16.9% of 1,244,944) in 2025; those moves are absent from this layer rather than distributed across it, so the country values do not sum to German migration. Departures are the weaker half of any register: a move out is recorded only if it is declared or later cleared administratively, which is why the unrecorded-destination share above is roughly twice the one on arrivals.

layers.title: Italian register: registrations from abroad, by country left
layers.question: How many people registered in Italy from this country in 2025?
layers.note: Italy's municipal population register (anagrafe), counted by country of previous or next residence. Every 2025 cell carries OBS_STATUS "p": these are provisional and ISTAT revises them. Emigration in particular is understood to be undercounted, because leaving the register requires the emigrant to enrol with AIRE at a consulate and many never do. The table is sparse rather than zero-filled: a country absent from this layer had no published cell, which is not the same as nobody arriving.

layers.title: Italian register: deregistrations for abroad, by country moved to
layers.question: How many people left the Italian register for this country in 2025?
layers.note: Italy's municipal population register (anagrafe), counted by country of previous or next residence. Every 2025 cell carries OBS_STATUS "p": these are provisional and ISTAT revises them. Emigration in particular is understood to be undercounted, because leaving the register requires the emigrant to enrol with AIRE at a consulate and many never do. Fewer countries appear here than on the arrivals layer because a destination with no published cell is absent, not zero.

layers.title: EU first residence permits
layers.question: How many first residence permits did this country issue?
layers.note: First permits are issued to non-EU citizens only, so a member state's own EU-citizen arrivals are absent by construction; full series runs 2008-2025. The four reason facets shipped alongside sum exactly to this total.

layers.title: EU first permits issued for employment
layers.question: How many first permits did this country issue for work?
layers.note: One of four disjoint reason facets that sum to eu-first-permits; first permits are issued to non-EU citizens only, so a member state's own EU-citizen arrivals are absent by construction; full series runs 2008-2025.

layers.title: EU first permits issued for family reasons
layers.question: How many first permits did this country issue for family reasons?
layers.note: One of four disjoint reason facets that sum to eu-first-permits; first permits are issued to non-EU citizens only, so a member state's own EU-citizen arrivals are absent by construction; full series runs 2008-2025.

layers.title: EU first permits issued for education
layers.question: How many first permits did this country issue for study?
layers.note: One of four disjoint reason facets that sum to eu-first-permits; first permits are issued to non-EU citizens only, so a member state's own EU-citizen arrivals are absent by construction; full series runs 2008-2025.

layers.title: EU first permits issued for other reasons
layers.question: How many first permits did this country issue for reasons other than work, family or study?
layers.note: One of four disjoint reason facets that sum to eu-first-permits; first permits are issued to non-EU citizens only, so a member state's own EU-citizen arrivals are absent by construction; full series runs 2008-2025.

layers.title: EU first residence permits by citizenship and issuing country
layers.question: How many first residence permits did this destination issue to citizens of this origin?
layers.note: These corridors fall short of the country total by exactly the stateless, recognised-non-citizen, unknown-citizenship and British-overseas-territory permits, which have no origin country to key on; a reported zero is kept as a zero, because absent and nil are different answers here.

layers.title: EU unemployment rate, 15-74
layers.question: What share of this country’s labour force was unemployed?
layers.note: A rate, so it must never be summed or area-weighted across countries; the flag ‘d’ that France and Spain carry means their definition differs from the rest and the gap is partly definitional.

layers.title: EU residence permits valid on 31 December
layers.question: How many residence permits were valid here at the end of the year?
layers.note: A stock of valid permits at a year end, not a flow: it moves with how long permits last as much as with how many were issued, so it must not be differenced against eu-first-permits.

layers.title: EU returns of non-EU citizens ordered to leave
layers.question: How many non-EU citizens returned after being ordered to leave this country?
layers.note: Eurostat rounds every value in this table to the nearest 5 for disclosure control — the dataset title says "(rounded)" — so small reporters carry rounding error of the same order as the count.

layers.title: Net migration
layers.question: Did more people arrive here than left, and by how many?
layers.note: Immigrants minus emigrants, citizens and non-citizens alike, so it is SIGNED: at 2025, 130 of 217 countries are negative and one is exactly zero. It is also the residual of UN World Population Prospects — the part of population change that births and deaths do not explain — not a counted flow, which is why a country can show a clean annual figure nobody ever measured. Two directions of the same size cancel to nothing here; a zero means balance, never absence.

layers.title: Unemployment rate
layers.question: What share of the labour force is out of work and looking?
layers.note: The indicator's own name ends "(modeled ILO estimate)": these are ILO model outputs harmonised across countries for comparability, not the national unemployment rates the same countries publish, and the two routinely differ. Coverage is the thinnest of this family — 182 of 217 countries at the newest period — so a blank here is a country the ILO does not model, not a country with no unemployment.

layers.title: Refugees hosted
layers.question: How many refugees is this country hosting?
layers.note: UNHCR-mandate refugees by country of asylum, including people in a refugee-like situation. MARGINAL TOTAL, NOT A MATRIX — see the shared warning below. A standing population reported once a year, not arrivals during the year: do not sum it across periods. Zero is a real value here (9 countries report zero at the newest period) and is not the same as a country that does not report. These are marginal totals of UNHCR's origin-by-asylum matrix, not the matrix. The asylum-side layers say how many people are here and nothing about where they came from; the origin-side layers say how many came from here and nothing about where they went. No corridor can be built from them, and the totals prove it: at 2025 the refugee margins are 28,461,306 by asylum against 28,112,534 by origin, and the asylum-seeker margins 8,998,091 against 7,419,988 — 21% apart, because a large share of claims are lodged by people whose origin is recorded as stateless, unknown or as an aggregate that is not a country. Pairing a row from one side with a row from the other invents the pairing.

layers.title: Refugees from here
layers.question: How many refugees originate from this country?
layers.note: The same UNHCR refugee population counted by country of ORIGIN instead of asylum. MARGINAL TOTAL, NOT A MATRIX — see the shared warning below. Origin coverage is wider than asylum coverage (198 against 176 at the newest period) because a country can produce refugees without hosting any. These are marginal totals of UNHCR's origin-by-asylum matrix, not the matrix. The asylum-side layers say how many people are here and nothing about where they came from; the origin-side layers say how many came from here and nothing about where they went. No corridor can be built from them, and the totals prove it: at 2025 the refugee margins are 28,461,306 by asylum against 28,112,534 by origin, and the asylum-seeker margins 8,998,091 against 7,419,988 — 21% apart, because a large share of claims are lodged by people whose origin is recorded as stateless, unknown or as an aggregate that is not a country. Pairing a row from one side with a row from the other invents the pairing.

layers.title: Asylum seekers hosted
layers.question: How many people are waiting on a claim in this country?
layers.note: People who have sought international protection and whose claims are undetermined, by country of asylum. MARGINAL TOTAL, NOT A MATRIX — see the shared warning below. A pending caseload is a queue length, not a flow: it grows with arrivals and shrinks with decisions, so a fall can mean fewer claims or faster processing and the number alone cannot tell you which. These are marginal totals of UNHCR's origin-by-asylum matrix, not the matrix. The asylum-side layers say how many people are here and nothing about where they came from; the origin-side layers say how many came from here and nothing about where they went. No corridor can be built from them, and the totals prove it: at 2025 the refugee margins are 28,461,306 by asylum against 28,112,534 by origin, and the asylum-seeker margins 8,998,091 against 7,419,988 — 21% apart, because a large share of claims are lodged by people whose origin is recorded as stateless, unknown or as an aggregate that is not a country. Pairing a row from one side with a row from the other invents the pairing.

layers.title: Asylum seekers from here
layers.question: How many people from this country are waiting on a claim somewhere?
layers.note: The pending caseload counted by country of ORIGIN. MARGINAL TOTAL, NOT A MATRIX — see the shared warning below, which matters most on this pair: the two asylum-seeker margins do not even sum to the same world total. These are marginal totals of UNHCR's origin-by-asylum matrix, not the matrix. The asylum-side layers say how many people are here and nothing about where they came from; the origin-side layers say how many came from here and nothing about where they went. No corridor can be built from them, and the totals prove it: at 2025 the refugee margins are 28,461,306 by asylum against 28,112,534 by origin, and the asylum-seeker margins 8,998,091 against 7,419,988 — 21% apart, because a large share of claims are lodged by people whose origin is recorded as stateless, unknown or as an aggregate that is not a country. Pairing a row from one side with a row from the other invents the pairing.

layers.title: Forcibly displaced people
layers.question: How many displaced people are inside this country's borders?
layers.note: UNHCR's own composite: refugees (and refugee-like situations) under UNHCR mandate, plus UNRWA refugees, plus asylum-seekers, plus others in need of international protection, plus internally displaced people, deduplicated by UNHCR where it can be. It is therefore ASYLUM-SIDE and dominated by IDPs in the largest cases — Colombia and Sudan lead it, and both are mostly people displaced inside their own country. It is not comparable with the origin-side layers and must not be differenced against them. The series starts at 2010; there is nothing before that. These are marginal totals of UNHCR's origin-by-asylum matrix, not the matrix. The asylum-side layers say how many people are here and nothing about where they came from; the origin-side layers say how many came from here and nothing about where they went. No corridor can be built from them, and the totals prove it: at 2025 the refugee margins are 28,461,306 by asylum against 28,112,534 by origin, and the asylum-seeker margins 8,998,091 against 7,419,988 — 21% apart, because a large share of claims are lodged by people whose origin is recorded as stateless, unknown or as an aggregate that is not a country. Pairing a row from one side with a row from the other invents the pairing.

layers.title: Population
layers.question: How many people live here?
layers.note: A denominator, not a headline. The World Bank's own sourceNote says "The values shown are midyear estimates" and lists UN World Population Prospects first among its sources, so this is a demographic model fitted to censuses and registers rather than a count — it is badged modelled for that reason, and all 217 countries carry a value in every single year this layer ships because the model has no gaps, not because everyone counted. De facto residents, regardless of legal status or citizenship.

layers.title: EU population on 1 January
layers.question: How many people lived here on 1 January?
layers.note: The denominator layer, not a migration measure: citizen=TOTAL on this table is the whole resident population.

layers.title: EU foreign citizens resident on 1 January
layers.question: How many residents here held foreign or no citizenship on 1 January?
layers.note: A citizenship stock, not a foreign-born stock: naturalised residents leave this count without moving, so it falls where naturalisation is easy and rises where it is not.

layers.title: EU immigration (population register)
layers.question: How many people did this country register as immigrating?
layers.note: Register immigration counts anyone taking up residence for 12 months or more, EU citizens included, so it is a wider quantity than a permit count and the two must not be differenced.

layers.title: EU emigration (population register)
layers.question: How many people did this country register as emigrating?
layers.note: Emigration is the worst-measured side of a register: a departure is reported by the person leaving, so these counts run low against the receiving country’s immigration figure for the same flow.

layers.title: Foreign-born stock by corridor
layers.question: How many people born in one country are living in another?
layers.note: Modelled, not counted. These are the migrant-stock estimates the flow model is fitted against, and they reach a year further than the flows do because the flow for a year is inferred from the change between two stock anchors. The model also fills in corridors the underlying tables never observed, so a corridor can carry a confident-looking number that nobody counted — the concordance page measures how large that filling-in is, country by country, against the UN DESA figures the model was fitted to. A stock is a standing population, not a movement: do not read a change between two anchors as a flow, and never sum stocks across years. This layer ships the 9,200 largest of 53,130 corridors — the top 25 on each side of every country — which is 97.6% of the estimated stock. The two country layers are summed over all of them and are not trimmed.

layers.title: Foreign-born population
layers.question: How many people living here were born somewhere else?
layers.note: Modelled, not counted. These are the migrant-stock estimates the flow model is fitted against, and they reach a year further than the flows do because the flow for a year is inferred from the change between two stock anchors. The model also fills in corridors the underlying tables never observed, so a corridor can carry a confident-looking number that nobody counted — the concordance page measures how large that filling-in is, country by country, against the UN DESA figures the model was fitted to. Summed over every origin, so it is the destination margin of the corridor layer rather than an independent measurement of it.

layers.title: People born here living abroad
layers.question: How many people born in this country are living somewhere else?
layers.note: Modelled, not counted. These are the migrant-stock estimates the flow model is fitted against, and they reach a year further than the flows do because the flow for a year is inferred from the change between two stock anchors. The model also fills in corridors the underlying tables never observed, so a corridor can carry a confident-looking number that nobody counted — the concordance page measures how large that filling-in is, country by country, against the UN DESA figures the model was fitted to. The origin margin of the same matrix. A country can be large on this layer and small on the foreign-born layer, or both at once.

layers.title: GDP per capita, PPP
layers.question: How much output per person does this economy produce, at comparable prices?
layers.note: National accounts as reported, converted with purchasing-power parities from the International Comparison Program. The PPPs are benchmarked on the 2021 ICP round and extrapolated to every other year, so the comparison across countries is a World Bank construction even though the underlying GDP is nationally reported. This is the one series in this adapter whose newest year is a year behind the others, and deliberately so: the year after the one shipped here exists in the API with roughly ten fewer countries, and is dropped rather than charted.

layers.title: Foreign-born population
layers.question: How many people living here were born somewhere else?
layers.note: UN DESA mid-year estimates of the number of people born in a country other than the one they live in, refugees included. NOT annual: the periods are 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020 and then 2024, so the gap either side of a point is years wide and the line between two points is drawn by the reader, not by the producer. A stock is a standing population — never sum it across periods, and never read the change between two of these as a flow.
